name: Kom
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Aimol, Chongom Damrengthang. 2007. A descriptive grammar of Kom. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Canchipur (supervisor S. Imoba Singh). xii+295 pp. Shodhganga hdl:10603/105232. Ch. II 'The phonological system', pp. 14-56.
catalog_locator: Ch. II sec. 2.0 'The phonological system', p. 14 and sec. 2.4 'Tone', p. 54 (pp. 2 and 41 of the chapter file); both pages read from the scan.
catalog_quote: p.14, sec. 2.0 THE PHONOLOGICAL SYSTEM: "The Kom language has twenty-seven principal phonemes. Out of the twenty-seven phonemes the number of segmental and suprasegmental phonemes are twenty-five and two respectively. Segmental phonemes include nineteen consonants– /p, pʰ, b, t, tʰ, d, c, k, kʰ, m, n, ŋ, r, v, s, h, l, w, and j/ and six vowels– /a, e, ə, i, o and u/. The two suprasegmental phonemes are level tone and falling tone. The phonemes of Kom can be classified as given below. 2.0.1. PHONEMES (A) Segmental phonemes a) Vowels (6) b) Consonants (19) (B) Supra-segmental phonemes a) Tones (2) i) Level tone ii) Falling tone" p.54, sec. 2.4 TONE: "Language that use the pitch of individual syllables to contrast meaning are called tone language. ... Tone is one of the main characteristics of Tibeto-Burman language. Many languages of Asia, such as Chinese, Thai, Burmese, etc. are tonal language. Only in Thai, therefore, have five tones. Kom has two tones as that of Manipuri has. Falling tone is marked by /ˋ/ and level tone which left unmarked. For instance: Level tone / Falling tone: ten "fishing net" / tèn "fishing net" (male); əkəjuŋ "flying" / əkəjùŋ "coming"; puŋ "gong" / pùŋ "hour"; in "house" / ìn "fishing net" (female); əkəteŋ "erode" / əkətèŋ "walk"; aj "crab" / àj "black rhizome"; mərsa "a kind of tree" / mə̀rsə "bag"; entuj "soup" / entùj "bamboo shoot"; tur "push" / tùr "poison""
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kom is described as a lexical tone language with a two-way tonal contrast on syllables (Aimol 2007 and Sucheta 1998: level vs falling; Kom 2009: high [slightly falling] vs low); the only suprasegmental phonemes recognised are the two tones. None of the three descriptions that treat Kom phonology mentions word stress or accent at all, either as contrastive or as predictable, so no stress-placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement). Concurring tonal statements: Kom, Karung Tarun 2009, ch.3 sec. 3.8.2, p.47 (file kom2010_nehu/): "Kom is a tonal language. Tone plays a very important role in the language as the same word may mean two or three different things with the changing of the tone. There are two register tones in Kom at the lexical level. They are – (i) high tone (╱) and (ii) low tone (╲). High tone is a tone with high pitch falling slightly and low tone is a tone with low pitch." Sucheta 1998 sec. 4.1.5 p.83: "In Kom, there are two tones, one is level tone and the other one is considered as falling tone."
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is assigned per syllable/lexical item in citation forms (mono- and disyllabic minimal pairs). Aimol 2007 is based on the Khoirentak Khunou village variety (Churachandpur district); Kom 2009 describes 'standard Kom' = the Mongtung variety; both note village-level dialect variation but mutual intelligibility.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary descriptions are of Kom proper (kmm, komi1270), not the Kolhreng/Koireng variety. Aimol 2007 data: Khoirentak Khunou village (Churachandpur district). Kom 2009/2010 phonology: 'standard Kom', i.e. the Mongtung variety (audio Bible plus two elderly Mongtung speakers); its ch.4 treats Mantak and other village varieties. Glottolog's Shultz 1997 SIL-Cameroon item belongs to Kom of Cameroon (Grassfields), not this language.

sources.note: Nothing. Phonology chapter covers vowels, consonants, clusters, syllable (2.3) and tone (2.4): 27 phonemes of which two are suprasegmental, 'level tone and falling tone' (p.14); 'Kom has two tones as that of Manipuri has' (p.54). Ch.1 p.1: 'It is an agglutinative as well as tonal language.' No section or remark on stress/accent anywhere in ch.1-2 (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent absent).

PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, North-Eastern Hill University, Shillong (supervisor J. War). Shodhgangahttp://hdl.handle.net/10603/5505.Ch. 3 'Phonology of Kom' (50 pp., text).
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. Sec. 3.8.2 'Tones in Kom' (p.47): 'Kom is a tonal language.. There are two register tones in Kom at the lexical level. They are – (i) high tone and (ii) low tone. High tone is a tone with high pitch falling slightly and low tone is a tone with low pitch', with minimal pairs (thái 'edible'/thài 'oil', túi 'tasty'/tùi 'water'..). Describes 'standard Kom' = Mongtung variety. 'stress' occurs only inside quoted definitions (Schane, sonority).

sources.citation: Sucheta, Elangbam. 1998. A grammatical comparison of Manipuri, Kom, Paite and Tangkhul. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University. Shodhgangahttp://hdl.handle.net/10603/105206.Ch. IV 'Kom phonology' pp. 76-87 (image scan, scanned).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 4.1.5 'Supra-Segmental' (p.83): 'In Kom, there are two tones, one is level tone and the other one is considered as falling tone', with pairs be 'pulse'/bè 'pitcher', in 'house'/ìn 'fishing net'. Suprasegmentals = tones only (the parallel Manipuri chapter has tones + junctures).
